course_goal: Enable new operations analysts to classify unfamiliar short time-series patterns and justify decisions without overclaiming from a single point or timing coincidence.

audience.description: New operations analysts who review weekly dashboards
prior_knowledge: Can read whole numbers and percentages
audience.work_context: Classifying dashboard patterns before escalating an operational issue
accessibility: Do not rely on color alone

terminal_objective.performance: Classify an unfamiliar short time-series as a trend, anomaly, or insufficient evidence and justify the decision with visible cues.
terminal_objective.condition: Given a labeled or partially labeled chart not used during modeling
success_criteria: Names at least one visible cue
Does not claim causation from timing alone

objectives.performance: Inspect title, axes, units, time span, and scale before interpreting a chart.
misconceptions: The line shape can be interpreted before reading labels
objectives.transfer_context: A chart with a different metric, scale, and missing unit label

evidence.description: Identify which missing or overlooked chart context makes a conclusion unsafe.

practices.description: Independently identify why an unlabeled chart cannot support a firm classification.

feedback.content: Missing context changes what the same line shape could mean, so the defensible category is insufficient evidence.

representations.rationale: A realistic analysis workspace anchors the chart-reading task in the learner's work context.
An annotated dashboard lets learners locate title, units, scale, and time span in a real interface.
A short ordered process gives novices a reusable inspection routine before classification.

objectives.performance: Distinguish a sustained trend from an isolated anomaly and from insufficient evidence.
objectives.condition: Given short time-series examples with varied surface features
success_criteria: Does not treat one point as a trend
misconceptions: Any large final point proves a trend
Every unusual point is an error
objectives.transfer_context: A staffing metric with a different range and direction from the worked example

evidence.description: Classify several unfamiliar patterns and cite the feature that separates them.
criteria: Evidence names persistence, return to range, or missing context

practices.description: Classify a short numeric sequence after a comparison of trend and anomaly.

feedback.content: A trend persists across observations; an anomaly departs and then returns toward the prior range.

practices.description: Independently classify a different downward sequence.

feedback.content: Direction can be upward or downward; repeated movement is the relevant cue.

representations.rationale: Plotted observations make persistence and return to the prior range directly inspectable.
Side-by-side criteria expose the decision boundary between a trend and an anomaly.
Progressively appearing observations demonstrate that a trend is established across time, not by one point.
The worked example makes the expert inspection and classification steps visible.

objectives.performance: Justify a pattern classification with visible evidence while separating an investigation hypothesis from a causal claim.
objectives.condition: Given an unfamiliar chart and a nearby operational event
success_criteria: Does not infer cause from timing alone
misconceptions: A nearby event proves what caused the pattern
Naming a category is enough justification
objectives.transfer_context: A hospital wait-time chart paired with a scheduling change

evidence.description: Classify and justify a new domain example while qualifying a causal hypothesis.

practices.description: Independently classify and justify an unfamiliar wait-time sequence.

feedback.content: A strong response names the category, cites repeated movement, and treats the scheduling change as a hypothesis rather than proof.

representations.rationale: A timeline makes temporal proximity visible while preserving the distinction between sequence and causation.
A novel chart supplies observable evidence for the final independent classification.

episodes.transfer_task: Classify and justify an unfamiliar hospital wait-time pattern paired with a nearby scheduling change.

follow_up.activity: Inspect and classify one unlabeled and one labeled chart before checking the guide.
Classify a new work dashboard pattern, cite evidence, and write one alternate explanation.

retention.interleaving_rationale: Trend, anomaly, and insufficient-evidence cases are mixed because analysts must discriminate among them in the same workflow.
